extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of mechanics and fluid physics (advanced undergraduate / graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains classical principles and conditions for equilibrium and motion of (weightless and ordinary) liquids: surface-tension/molecular-force effects, mean-curvature equilibrium (Plateau/Clairaut/Gauss), bubbles and films, potential-force conditions, and efflux (Torricelli/Bernoulli) relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Molecular forces act only in superficial film
rubrics_metrics.description: Molecular forces of a liquid act only at very small distances and are effectively restricted to a superficial stratum (the liquid's film); gravity may be neglected in a weightless-liquid idealization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies treating the energetic effects of molecular forces as associated with the surface only (Plateau experiments and soap films). The interior particles experience zero resultant molecular force if uniformly surrounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work is done only by change of surface area
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveying a particle within the bulk interior (from one interior position to another) does no net work; work can be done only by transferring particles between the superficial stratum and the interior, i.e., by a change in the surface size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore energy considerations for molecular forces reduce to variations of superficial area. This underpins the use of virtual displacements that change surface area to test equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminution of surface area produces positive work
rubrics_metrics.description: When two fluid drops coalesce or a soap film contracts, the resulting diminution of superficial area corresponds to positive work done by molecular forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental illustration: a soap-film inside a loop contracts to a circular boundary (maximizes enclosed area for given perimeter), showing the system tends to minimize surface area and that reduction of area releases energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium criterion via virtual displacements of surface area
rubrics_metrics.description: A weightless liquid under molecular forces is in equilibrium for all virtual displacements that produce no alteration of the liquid's superficial area; for fixed volume, a minimum of superficial area gives stable equilibrium while a maximum gives unstable equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use virtual-displacement arguments constrained by constant volume to identify equilibrium shapes (variation of total surface area = 0 for admissible displacements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Free liquid assumes spherical form (area minimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all solids of the same volume the sphere has the least superficial area; therefore a free (unbounded, nonadhering) liquid mass assumes the spherical form in stable equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the geometric consequence of the minimum-area equilibrium principle; adherence to solids or other constraints changes the shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean-curvature (1/r + 1/r') constant over surface in equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: For a liquid surface in equilibrium under molecular forces (and constant volume), the sum of the reciprocals of the principal radii of curvature (i.e., the mean curvature) is constant over the whole free surface: 1/r + 1/r' = const.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the first-variation of surface area under the constraint of fixed volume (virtual displacement analysis). This is the fundamental equation linking surface curvature and equilibrium shape (Gauss/Clairaut reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of mean curvature determines specific meridian shapes
rubrics_metrics.description: The numerical value of 1/r + 1/r' (the mean curvature) for a surface of revolution fixes the meridian curve and the enclosed volume for given boundary rings; special values give cylinders or catenary-like curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: certain values cause the surface of revolution to become cylindrical; when one normal section is convex and the other concave with 1/r + 1/r' = 0 the meridian is a catenary. Plateau verified these experimentally with oil between rings in alcohol-water mixture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex and concave parts move to equalize mean curvature
rubrics_metrics.description: When a connected liquid surface has parts with different signs/values of 1/r + 1/r', convex parts are forced inward and concave parts outward until the condition 1/r + 1/r' = const is fulfilled everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence surfaces with varying curvature will evolve (flow) to redistribute surface area and reach uniform mean curvature across free portions, subject to constraints and boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated surface-parts must share same mean curvature in equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: If a connected liquid mass has several isolated free surface parts (bounded by rigid bodies), the value of 1/r + 1/r' must be the same for all free portions of the surface in equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures no net flow between isolated portions; experimental consequence: oil columns between rings may form cylindrical lateral surface with spherical caps when parameters satisfy the curvature relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hollow cavities collapse unless internal pressure balances surface work
rubrics_metrics.description: A hollow space inside a liquid cannot have interior and exterior surfaces with the same mean curvature; the liquid will tend to flow to eliminate the hollow unless the internal cavity is filled with a fluid/gas exerting sufficient pressure to counteract the work associated with surface-area change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equilibrium can be established if the work done by surface changes is compensated by the work required to compress the interior substance (pressure-volume work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bubble pressure–surface-work relation (Young–Laplace style)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a thin spherical bubble the work per unit diminution of surface (A) and the pressure p of the inclosed gas are related by the derived relation A/r = p (text's stated form); measuring r and p allows computation of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text shows the derivation by equating decrease of surface-work to compression work p·(volume change). (In modern form for a single interface γ: p = 2γ/R for a thin spherical interface; the text's A corresponds to the surface 'work per unit area' parameter.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Open bubbles and minimal surfaces: mean curvature zero
rubrics_metrics.description: An open bubble (soap film spanning wire contours) in equilibrium must have 1/r + 1/r' = 0 for each of the two bounding surfaces (opposite curvatures), i.e., the surface is a minimal surface with zero mean curvature and saddle-shaped elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimal surfaces are those of least area given boundary contours (Plateau's problem); soap films experimentally realize such minimal surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plateau film junction rules (empirical geometric constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thin liquid films (soap films) connected to wire frames meet one another in threes at approximately equal angles of 120°, and in fours at corners with approximately equal angles, corresponding to minimal-area geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the fundamental mean-curvature equation may not hold exactly for very thin/viscous films, these junction angle rules are robust geometric consequences of area minimization observed in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry and regularity favor equilibrium forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetry in a system causes deformations destroying symmetry to be counterbalanced by opposite deformations; thus symmetric/regular forms often correspond to maxima or minima of the work and hence are typical equilibrium shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetry is a sufficient (though not strictly necessary) ingredient explaining why many equilibrium configurations are regular or symmetric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clairaut's general condition: forces derive from potential function U
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary condition for liquid equilibrium under body forces is that the force components X, Y, Z be expressible as the partial derivatives of the same scalar function U (i.e., Xdx + Ydy + Zdz must be a complete differential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition implies that pressure differences depend only on end-point positions, not on path; it is the foundational requirement for treating forces via a potential (force-function) in hydrostatics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure is a function of potential for conservative forces
rubrics_metrics.description: For forces that are gradients of a potential U (central forces like gravity), dp = ρ dU, and therefore pressure p = ρ U + const; equipotential surfaces U = const are isobaric (constant pressure) surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This links the mechanical force field to hydrostatic pressure distribution: knowing U gives both force directions (normal to equipotentials) and pressure relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equipotential/level-surface geometry and force direction
rubrics_metrics.description: On a level (equipotential) surface U = const the tangential components of resultant force vanish and the resultant force is everywhere normal to the surface; the force magnitude between nearby equipotentials is inversely proportional to the distance between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus field lines are curves everywhere orthogonal to equipotential surfaces; the spacing of equipotentials gives the local strength of the force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-potential forces produce steady circulation (no hydrostatic equilibrium)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the body forces cannot be expressed as derivatives of a scalar potential (i.e., Xdx + Ydy + Zdz is not a complete differential), a liquid cannot be at rest in closed canals and will exhibit persistent rotational currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: chosen force components that violate the equality of mixed partials produce net work around closed paths and hence continuous circulation rather than equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torricelli / Bernoulli efflux principle (energy/momentum viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting resistances, the velocity v of efflux of a liquid through an orifice at the bottom of a vessel with head h satisfies v = sqrt(2 g h); this is equivalent to the final velocity of a freely falling body through height h and can be derived by momentum (Varignon) or energy/vis viva (Bernoulli) arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivations: (a) Varignon-type momentum balance leads to v^2 = 2 g h; (b) Bernoulli / vis viva equates potential energy release q·dh·s·h to kinetic energy of discharged fluid yielding v = sqrt(2 g h). Practical derivations may include correction factors for resistances.
